item.title: Issue 8: Keep the human in the loop.
item.description: The APA Education Committee hand-sifted 2,996 abstracts to name the 11 must-read med ed papers of 2025. Meanwhile, most IM clerkships still have no clear AI policy, a medical school study finds that early struggles predict later ones (and need more than academic fixes), and a new essay asks how we grow after we get it wrong. item.title: Issue 7: Take care of the whole learner.
item.description: Nearly 1 in 3 trainees at one big academic center screened food insecure, with interns hit hardest. Elsewhere this week: a 90-minute workshop that makes students more confident teachers, a review showing we barely teach how to say "I'm not sure," and new Academic Pediatrics pieces on handover and source-grounded AI at the bedside. item.title: Issue 6: Fix the system, not the learner.
item.description: This week's papers keep pointing at structures: grading committees and longitudinal clerkships shrink some Honors gaps, early low-stakes monitoring plans go with fewer formal remediation plans, and the JD-R model reframes trainee burnout as a demands-vs-resources problem on the wards. Meanwhile, AI could help with every piece of CBME, if we evaluate it honestly. item.title: Issue 5: Our trainees are already using AI. Now what?
item.description: A huge JAMA study shows residents and early-career doctors are the heaviest users of an AI clinical tool, and a companion Viewpoint asks what we should still teach once the machine can answer. Back in the analog world, a concept-map rubric may spot struggling students early, and faculty burnout ranges from 13% to 41% across schools, so some places are doing something right. item.title: Issue 4: Who (and what) is in the room with our learners?
item.description: Generative AI is now a reasoning partner at the bedside, so the authors of this week's top read argue we should teach and supervise the learner-AI pair, with graduated autonomy, not just the learner. Coaches who keep students tied to their values ease the jump to residency. And a growing share of the doctors our residents train beside come from Caribbean schools, most into primary care. item.title: Issue 3: Safe to struggle, safe to say so.
item.description: A new 5-item scale offers a quick check on whether trainees feel safe sharing ideas, uncertainty, and mistakes. Residents who went through remediation echo it: transparency and personalization make or break the process. And as EHR metrics like TRACERs reveal each resident's practice patterns, how we share that data matters as much as the data. item.title: Issue 2: "Ready" has to be proven now.
item.description: The ABP just opened a 2-year fellowship path in 7 subspecialties for programs that can show readiness with EPAs. That makes trustworthy assessment data priceless, and a JGME study finds AI summaries of rotation comments catch most strengths but miss most areas for improvement. On the recruitment side, signals dominate who gets an interview, and a small PHM pilot shows how far a structured mentoring cohort can move confidence. item.title: Issue 1: "Ready for what?"
item.description: Pediatric PDs feel a heavy moral duty to call graduates practice-ready but define readiness differently, just as the ABP moves to EPA-based attestations in 2028. On the way in, pediatrics-specific signals (the NBME shelf, clerkship honors, GHHS) modestly predict early Milestones. Once residents arrive, the hidden struggles are about adapting to the workplace, and Academic Pediatrics shows how help-seeking and autonomy develop along the way.
